description: An island of 36,000 km² makes most of the world's electronic chips. That is why **Taiwan** is one of the most dangerous places on the planet.

hero.hook: A small island makes the chips that keep the whole world running, and Beijing claims it as a province.

blocks.text: **Taiwan** is seen as one of the most dangerous flashpoints of the 21st century. For China, the island is only a rebel province that must one day “return” to the national fold. For its 23 million inhabitants, it is a sovereign democracy, born of a civil war the rest of the world has almost forgotten.

Beyond questions of identity, Taiwan has become the beating heart of the global digital economy. That is what makes an armed conflict there so frightening: it would threaten not just Asia, but every factory and every smartphone on the planet.

It all began with the **Chinese Civil War**, which set Mao Zedong's communists against the nationalists of the **[[Kuomintang]]**, led by Chiang Kai-shek. In 1949, crushed by the communist victory, the nationalists fled to the island of Taiwan, taking with them the treasures of the Forbidden City and the machinery of their state.

blocks.caption: In 1949, the Kuomintang nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan after their defeat by the communists

blocks.text: For decades, two governments fought over the title of sole legitimate representative of China. The turning point came in 1971, when the UN took the seat away from Taipei and gave it to Beijing. Taiwan was left diplomatically isolated, yet it kept its own currency, its own army and an elected government.
The Kuomintang carried off so much art when it fled the mainland in 1949 that the National Palace Museum in Taipei now holds one of the richest collections of Chinese art in the world.

sections.title: The legacy of 1949: two rival Chinas

blocks.text: Cut off diplomatically, Taiwan pulled off a spectacular economic transformation. The island specialized in high technology, and in 1987 it created **[[TSMC]]**, now the heart of the global semiconductor industry, with more than 90% of the most advanced chips.

blocks.caption: TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced chips in Taiwan

blocks.text: This dominance creates a “silicon shield.” The whole world depends so heavily on Taiwanese factories that an invasion would paralyze production lines everywhere, from artificial intelligence to carmaking.

That success came with a major political shift. After decades of authoritarian rule, Taiwan became one of the most liberal democracies in Asia. In 1996, its first elections by **direct universal suffrage** marked a clean break with the Chinese model.

sections.title: The silicon shield: TSMC and the global stake

blocks.text: Taiwan's survival rests on a subtle diplomatic game run from Washington. Since a law passed in 1979, the United States has practiced **[[American strategic ambiguity]]**: it officially recognizes Beijing, but gives Taiwan the means to defend itself, without ever saying clearly whether it would step in militarily if the island were attacked.

This fragile balance has two aims: to deter Beijing from attacking for fear of an American response, and to deter Taipei from declaring formal independence, which would trigger war. But the balance is tested more and more often by Chinese military aircraft flying into the island's air defense identification zone, the **ADIZ**.

blocks.caption: Chinese military flights into Taiwanese airspace have multiplied in recent years

blocks.text: Xi Jinping's speeches worry observers, because he insists the Taiwan question cannot be handed down to later generations forever. The United States, for its part, has slowly been making its support more explicit, which raises the risk of a direct clash between the two superpowers.

The conflict is no longer only about missiles. It has spread to cyberspace and disinformation. Taiwan absorbs millions of cyberattacks every day, all aimed at shaking its democracy. The stake is symbolic too: Taiwan proves that a Chinese society can thrive under a democratic government.

Economic interdependence complicates everything: China is still the island's biggest trading partner, which slows any escalation. Among young Taiwanese, the feeling of belonging to a separate nation keeps growing, while Beijing has hardened its diplomacy since it forced Hong Kong back into line.
In 2021, after China banned its fruit, Taiwan launched the “freedom pineapple” campaign: people bought local pineapples in huge quantities and turned the fruit into a symbol of resistance.
Taiwan is the great geopolitical paradox of our time: a territory the UN does not recognize, yet one that every major power now depends on for its technology and its economy.

title: Tensions over Taiwan
